name: Merzouga and the Sahara
tagline: Golden dunes up to 150 metres high on the edge of the Sahara, reached by camel at dusk, with a night in a tented camp and a sunrise over the sand.
highlight: Watching the sunrise from the top of the highest dune at Erg Chebbi.
shortDescription: The gateway to Erg Chebbi, Morocco's biggest sand sea: camel treks, desert camps, Gnawa music and starry skies at the far end of the country.
metaDescription: A Merzouga and Sahara travel guide: Erg Chebbi dunes, camel treks, desert camps, Rissani, Khamlia, how to get there, what to pack, the best time to go and a two-day plan.
knownFor: Erg Chebbi dunes, camel treks, desert camps, night skies
budget: US$80–200 per person for a desert night with transfers

image.alt: The orange sand dunes of Erg Chebbi near Merzouga in the Moroccan Sahara

intro: Merzouga is a small village at the edge of Erg Chebbi, a sea of sand about 22 km long and 5 km wide that rises to roughly 150 metres in places. It sits close to the Algerian border, in the far south-east of Morocco, about as far from Tangier as it is possible to be in the country. It is the most accessible large dune field in Morocco and the classic Saharan experience.

The tradition is to leave the village in the late afternoon on a camel, follow a Berber guide into the dunes and arrive at a tented camp as the sun goes down. The evening involves dinner, music and drumming around a fire, and clear skies with a great many stars. The next morning, climbing a dune to watch the sunrise is the reward.

The village and its surroundings also have a life of their own. Local Gnawa communities in Khamlia perform music descended from West African traditions, Rissani has a busy market and the tombs of the Alaouite dynasty's ancestors, and nomads still camp near the dunes.

whyVisit.intro: Merzouga gives a memorable night in the Sahara without requiring days of trekking.

points.title: Real dunes
points.text: Erg Chebbi is a proper sand sea, with towering, ever-shifting dunes and sweeping curves.

points.title: The camel trek
points.text: A slow ride into the dunes at dusk is one of the most iconic experiences in Morocco.

points.title: Sunrise and stars
points.text: With little light pollution, the night sky is spectacular, and dawn on the dunes is memorable.

points.title: Local music and culture
points.text: Gnawa musicians, Amazigh hospitality and the desert markets at Rissani.

points.title: Adventure options
points.text: Sandboarding, 4x4 excursions and walking in the dunes.

attractionsIntro: The main event is the dunes, and the surroundings add variety over a couple of days.

attractions.name: Erg Chebbi
attractions.text: The sea of dunes, which reaches its greatest height near the Merzouga side. The sand is fine and orange, turning red at sunset.
attractions.tip: Climb the highest dune for sunrise, and bring a scarf against the wind.

attractions.name: A desert camp
attractions.text: A camp of tents in the dunes, from simple Berber tents to luxury tents with private bathrooms. Dinner and music are included.
attractions.tip: Check whether winter tents are heated, and whether the camp is on the dunes or at the edge.

attractions.name: Khamlia village
attractions.text: A village of Gnawa people, descended from sub-Saharan Africans, who perform trance music and drumming.
attractions.tip: Give a fair tip to the musicians.

attractions.name: Rissani
attractions.text: The historic market town, the ancestral home of the Alaouite dynasty and site of the ancient trading city of Sijilmassa, with a lively souk on market days.
attractions.tip: Go on a Tuesday, Thursday or Sunday for the main market.

attractions.name: Dayet Srji (the seasonal lake)
attractions.text: A seasonal lake by the dunes that fills after heavy rain and attracts flamingos and other birds.
attractions.tip: Ask locally whether it has water.

thingsToDoIntro: A camel trek and a night in the dunes are the main thing, with a few extras.

thingsToDo.title: Ride a camel at sunset
thingsToDo.text: About an hour and a half's ride into the dunes, guided by a local.
thingsToDo.tip: Wear long trousers and a scarf.

thingsToDo.title: Sleep in a camp
thingsToDo.text: Dinner, drums and stars, then breakfast at dawn.
thingsToDo.tip: Bring a torch and warm layers.

thingsToDo.title: Watch the sunrise from a dune
thingsToDo.text: Climb up before dawn and watch the sand change colour.

thingsToDo.title: Try sandboarding
thingsToDo.text: Sledding down the dunes on a board, an easy family activity.

thingsToDo.title: Take a 4x4 tour
thingsToDo.text: A drive through the desert hamlets, the lake and the Gnawa village.
thingsToDo.tip: Book with a reputable operator, and consider the environmental impact of quad bikes.

thingsToDo.title: Stargaze
thingsToDo.text: On a clear night, the Milky Way is visible without effort.
thingsToDo.tip: Avoid nights with a full moon.

foodIntro: Desert food is simple and hearty, based on bread, meat and vegetables.

foods.name: Berber pizza (madfouna)
foods.text: A folded bread stuffed with meat, onions and spices and baked in the sand.
foods.whereToTry: Local restaurants in Rissani and Merzouga.

foods.name: Tagine
foods.text: The staple, cooked with lamb, chicken or vegetables.

foods.name: Dates
foods.text: Sweet dates from the nearby oases.

foods.name: Mint tea
foods.text: The universal welcome, drunk in the dunes.

foods.name: Couscous
foods.text: Served on Fridays and for special occasions.

accommodation.intro: Most visitors stay one night in the desert and a night in a hotel or kasbah in Merzouga.

areas.name: A desert camp
areas.text: Basic Berber tents or luxury tents deep in the dunes.

areas.name: Merzouga village
areas.text: Kasbah-style hotels with pools at the foot of the dunes.

budget.label: Basic camp
budget.value: US$40–80 per person, with dinner and breakfast

gettingThere.intro: Merzouga is remote. The drive is part of the experience.

options.text: About 9 hours by road through the Middle Atlas and the Ziz Valley.
About 9 hours via Ouarzazate and the Dadès and Todra gorges, ideally over two days.
Multi-day tours from Fes and Marrakech include the desert night.
options.detail: Check group size and what is included.

options.text: Buses run to Erfoud and Rissani, and Errachidia airport has limited flights.

gettingAround.intro: Within Merzouga, everything is arranged by your camp or hotel.

options.text: The classic way to reach a camp.
Used for excursions and to reach remote camps.
Walking in the dunes is possible, but keep to marked tracks and go with someone.

bestTime.headline: October–April
bestTime.summary: The Sahara is scorching in summer and cold at night in winter. Spring and autumn are best.

seasons.text: Warm days, cool nights and clear skies. Sandstorms are possible.
Hot in September, then pleasant from October.
Pleasant days but cold nights, near freezing.

bestTime.avoid: June to August, when the desert heat is extreme.

itinerary.title: Two days in the Sahara
itinerary.intro: A night in the dunes and a morning to enjoy the surroundings.

days.title: Arrive and ride into the dunes
days.afternoon: A camel ride to the camp at sunset.

days.title: Sunrise and the surroundings
days.morning: Sunrise from the dunes, and breakfast.
days.evening: A rest or an onward drive.

tipsIntro: A few things prepare you for the desert.
tips: Do not plan Merzouga as a day trip. The desert experience needs a night.
Pack layers. Nights are cold in winter, even after a hot day.
Bring a scarf for the sun, wind and sand, and sunglasses.
Take a small bag for the camel ride. Larger luggage stays in the hotel.
Read reviews of camps and check that tents are private.
Take cash for tips and small purchases.

faq.q: How long do you need in Merzouga?
faq.a: At least one night in the dunes, with arrival the previous evening or a full day to reach it.

faq.q: Is it worth the long drive?
faq.a: For most visitors, yes. The dunes are a highlight. If time is short, the Agafay Desert near Marrakech is a stony alternative.
The main tourist area is well organised. Go with a reputable guide, and avoid the border area.
Comfortable long clothes, a scarf, sturdy shoes and warm layers for the evening.
Conditions vary. Choose operators who look after their animals, and ask about their care.

faq.q: Can I see the desert without a camel?
faq.a: Yes, by 4x4 or on foot, though the camel is the traditional way.
